source: Norman, Sherbino, Dore, Wood, Young, Gaissmaier, Kreuger, Monteiro (2014) The etiology of diagnostic errors: a controlled trial of System 1 versus System 2 reasoning
finding: Telling residents to be careful and reflective did not beat telling them to be fast. Wrong cases took longer than right cases.
numbers: Second-year residents, 20 computer internal-medicine cases. Speed cohort 2010 n=96, accuracy 44.5%, 69 s per case. Reflect cohort 2011 n=108, accuracy 45.0%, 89 s per case (p<.001 for time). Incorrect cases took about 17 s longer than correct in both cohorts.
limits: Abstract only read. Cohorts were different years, not randomised. Instructions change speed, not necessarily the process. Accuracy only about 45%, so knowledge was the limit.
agent_relevance: A prompt that says 'think slowly and carefully' is not an intervention that works. S0 mode choice should not rest on a slow-down instruction; use difficulty or a signal. Supports G1 and G11.

source: Sherbino, Kulasegaram, Howey, Norman (2014) Ineffectiveness of cognitive forcing strategies to reduce biases in diagnostic reasoning: a controlled trial
finding: Teaching cognitive forcing strategies to medical students changed nothing on bias-prone cases.
numbers: 191 students (145 trained, 46 control). Search-satisficing cases: 52% vs 48% started a search for a second diagnosis (p=0.91); 54% vs 48% found it (p=0.13). Availability cases: 45% in both groups found the uncommon diagnosis (p=0.98). False-positive cases: 64% vs 77% over-searched (p=0.12).
limits: Abstract only read. Novices; one 4-week rotation; vignette test, not real practice. Training may have been too short.
agent_relevance: Telling a model to 'watch for bias X' is the same kind of intervention. Prefer knowledge or checks that code can run. Supports section 4b (do not add a bias-awareness step).

source: Norman, Monteiro, Sherbino, Ilgen, Schmidt, Mamede (2017) The causes of errors in clinical reasoning: cognitive biases, knowledge deficits, and dual process thinking
finding: Errors come from both Type 1 and Type 2. Bias can be induced in the lab (availability most clearly), but its share of real errors is not shown. Bias-recognition teaching fails; knowledge reorganisation helps a little.
numbers: No pooled effect size in the abstract. Verdict: bias-recognition training ineffective; knowledge-based strategies 'small but consistent benefits'.
quote: Educational strategies directed at the recognition of biases are ineffective in reducing errors
limits: Abstract only read. Narrative review, not a meta-analysis. Authors are the main group arguing this view, so it is one school.
agent_relevance: The default-interventionist story (fast = error, slow = fix) is not the model to build S0 on. Treat the mode as a cost choice, and fix errors with knowledge and checks.

source: Pelaccia, Sherbino, Wyer, Norman (2025) Diagnostic reasoning and cognitive error in emergency medicine: implications for teaching and learning
finding: Contrasts a process-based dual-process view (System 1 bias, System 2 fixes) with a knowledge-based view (both systems run on stored cases). Argues the evidence favours the second. Slowing down and debiasing do not raise accuracy.
numbers: Residents and staff saw ECGs and chest X-rays for 175 to 1000 ms: accuracy about 0.70 to 0.83, small rise with time. Diagnosis from 1 to 20 s: true-positive rate rose slightly with time but so did false positives, so accuracy was nearly flat from 5 to 20 s. Zwaan et al: physicians could not agree above chance on which biases were present, and found twice as many biases when the case ended with a wrong diagnosis.
quote: such teaching approaches are not supported by research into the nature of diagnostic reasoning
limits: Narrative review by authors who hold one side; numbers are second-hand citations. Mostly emergency medicine and vignettes.
agent_relevance: Hindsight inflates bias labels: an LLM judge that 'finds biases' in a wrong trace is not evidence (G10). Supports no bias-hunting step. Recommends feeding the model relevant cases and knowledge, which fits retrieval grounding.

source: van den Berg, Zwaan, Mamede et al. (2021) The relationship between time to diagnose and diagnostic accuracy among internal medicine residents: a randomized experiment
finding: Within the same residents, correct diagnoses came faster than wrong ones. The attempt to induce availability bias failed.
numbers: 117 residents, multi-centre within-subject. Correct 115 s vs incorrect 129 s (p<.001). Bias diagnoses 115 s vs correct 115 s (p=.971) vs other errors 136 s (p=.082), exploratory. No significant availability-bias effect, so the main comparison was correct vs all errors.
limits: Failed bias induction means the key test could not be run. Time is confounded with case difficulty. Small exploratory trend for bias errors.
agent_relevance: Do not use long reasoning as a sign of care. Long traces are a sign of trouble (matches Moell 2025 and Wu 2025 for LLMs). Supports G11 and a cap on reasoning length.

source: Mamede, van Gog, van den Berge, Rikers, van Saase, van Guldener, Schmidt (2010) Effect of availability bias and reflective reasoning on diagnostic accuracy among internal medicine residents
finding: Availability bias was induced in second-year residents, and structured reflection fixed it. First-year residents did not show the bias.
numbers: 36 residents (18 first-year, 18 second-year). Second-years scored 1.55 (CI 1.15 to 1.96) on cases similar to earlier ones vs 2.19 (1.73 to 2.66) on others (p=.03). Reflection raised similar-case scores to 2.03 (second-years) and 2.31 (first-years), main effect p=.006. Biased earlier diagnosis given 1.44 vs 0.72 times (p=.04).
limits: Abstract only read. Small sample, one site. Reflection was structured reanalysis of findings, not a general 'think harder'. Interaction with training year suggests a knowledge effect.
agent_relevance: Reflection that reanalyses given findings and lists evidence for and against works where an instruction to slow down does not. Fits G2: revise from located evidence. Bias here came from a prior case in context, like contamination across attempts (S3 fresh context).

source: Mamede, de Carvalho-Filho, de Faria, Franci, Nunes, Tio, Rikers, Schmidt (2012) Reflection as a strategy to foster medical students' acquisition of diagnostic competence
finding: Structured reflection while practising cases hurt at first, then helped a week later. A learning effect, not a speed-accuracy trade.
numbers: 46 Year-4 students. Immediate test: reflection 0.48 vs differential 0.62 (p=.012) and immediate diagnosis 0.61 (p=.04). One week later: reflection 0.66 vs 0.48 (p<.01) and 0.52 (p=.01).
limits: Abstract only read. Single study, delayed test only 1 week. Effect is on learning new cases, not on in-the-moment accuracy.
agent_relevance: Reflection pays through what is stored, not through the immediate answer. For a no-training agent, the analogue is writing up verified lessons (memory), not adding a reflect step at inference.

source: Ilgen, Bowen, McIntyre, Eva et al. (2013) Comparing diagnostic performance and the utility of clinical vignette-based assessment under testing conditions designed to encourage either automatic or analytic thought
finding: First-impression instructions gave the same accuracy as directed systematic search.
numbers: 393 clinicians (students, trainees, faculty), randomised. Instruction effect F(1,379)=2.44, p=.12 (no difference). Complexity F=965.2, experience F=39.6, both p<.001. First-impression scores tracked USMLE more closely and reached alpha 0.75 with fewer items.
limits: Abstract only read. Vignettes, not live care. Null result from one design.
agent_relevance: Case complexity and experience drive accuracy, not the instruction. Mode should be set by difficulty, not by a blanket rule. Supports G12.

source: Lambe, Mulrooney, Seemungal, Pancharatnam et al. (2018) Dual-process cognitive interventions to enhance diagnostic reasoning: a systematic review
finding: Of 28 intervention studies, guided reflection was most consistently successful (5 studies). Cognitive forcing strategies raised accuracy and confidence in some studies. Evidence is mixed and heterogeneous.
numbers: 28 studies in five categories: education, checklists, cognitive forcing, guided reflection, instructions at test. No pooled effect size reported in abstract.
limits: Abstract only read. Systematic review without a pooled estimate. Mostly early-career doctors. This conflicts with Sherbino 2014 and shows the field is not settled.
agent_relevance: The one family that works most often is guided reflection on the actual findings, not generic slowing. Keep S5 revision tied to located failing output (G2).

source: Evans and Stanovich (2013) Dual-process theories of higher cognition: advancing the debate
finding: Defends the dual-process split against five lines of criticism. Concedes some critiques hit some versions. Defines Type 2 by working-memory load and hypothetical thinking, not by speed. Keeps the default-interventionist idea: Type 1 gives the default unless Type 2 intervenes.
numbers: No data; theory paper.
quote: What defines the difference is that Type 2 processing supports hypothetical thinking and load heavily on working memory.
limits: Abstract only read. Authors defend their own framework.
agent_relevance: Gives the cleanest definition: Type 2 is what uses working memory and supposition. In an LLM this maps to written intermediate steps. Speed alone is not the marker.

source: Bago and De Neys (2017) Fast logic?: examining the time course assumption of dual process theory
finding: With load and deadlines to block deliberation, people still often gave the correct logical answer as their first, fast answer. This runs against the default-interventionist time course (wrong fast, right slow).
numbers: Four experiments, two-response paradigm (quick answer, then free time). Correct first answers were frequent, fast and confident despite a conflicting heuristic. Exact percentages not read this session.
limits: Abstract only read. Reasoning problems (bat and ball, syllogism, base rate), not diagnosis. Some critics say load did not fully stop Type 2.
agent_relevance: Fast does not mean wrong. A direct answer can be correct without deliberation, so S0 should not send everything to slow mode. Direct mode is a valid default for easy items (G11, G12).

source: Thompson, Prowse Turner, Pennycook (2011) Intuition, reason, and metacognition
finding: A fast Feeling of Rightness (FOR) on the first answer predicts how much people rethink. Low FOR led to longer rethinking and more answer changes. FOR was predicted by how fluently the first answer came.
numbers: Four experiments: conditional reasoning n=60, three-term conditional n=48, base-rate n=128, syllogisms n=64.
limits: Abstract only read. Fluency is also a source of overconfidence, so FOR is a cue, not a guarantee.
agent_relevance: This is the human version of an impasse signal. For an LLM the nearest measurable signal is disagreement across independent attempts or failed checks, not stated confidence (SCHEMA section 4b on verbal confidence).

source: Pennycook, Fugelsang, Koehler (2015) What makes us think? A three-stage dual-process model of analytic engagement
finding: Proposes three stages: Type 1 cues, conflict detection, then Type 2 as rationalisation or decoupling. Conflict detection sometimes fails, and detection and decoupling are separate sources of error.
numbers: Base-rate task with conflict vs non-conflict problems; sample sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only read. Reasoning-lab task, not clinical.
agent_relevance: Two separate failures: not noticing a conflict, and noticing but not overriding. A scaffold needs code that creates the conflict signal (a check or disagreement), as the model may not notice it alone.

source: De Neys (2012/2015) Bias and conflict: a case for logical intuitions
finding: Reasoners who give biased answers still show signs of detecting that the heuristic answer conflicts with logic (slower, less confident). So logic is partly intuitive.
numbers: Review of conflict-detection studies; no single effect size in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only read. Some of this depends on small differences in confidence and latency.
agent_relevance: A wrong answer can still carry a warning signal. If the agent varies across samples, that is a usable trigger for slow mode.

source: Kahneman and Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Intuition is trustworthy when the environment is regular enough to predict and the person had long practice with feedback. Feeling confident is not a guide to accuracy.
numbers: No data; joint paper by the two schools.
quote: Subjective experience is not a reliable indicator of judgment accuracy.
limits: Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Mode rule for S0: use fast answers where the task class has fast, reliable feedback and the model has shown success; otherwise run checks. Matches G12.

source: Bouwmeester, Verkoeijen, Aczel et al. (2017) Registered Replication Report: Rand, Greene, and Nowak (2012)
finding: Large preregistered replication of the claim that fast decisions are more cooperative. The main analysis found essentially no effect. The effect appeared only among participants who complied with the time limit, which points to selection.
numbers: 21 labs. Intent-to-treat difference -0.37 percentage points (original 8.6). Compliant-only 10.37 points (original 15.31). Non-compliance: 65.9% in time pressure, 7.5% in forced delay. Earlier meta-analysis cited: 51 studies, N=15,850, heterogeneous.
quote: consistent with the presence of selection biases and the absence of a causal effect of time pressure on cooperation
limits: This tests a social-heuristics claim in economic games, not diagnosis. Time-pressure manipulation had poor compliance.
agent_relevance: Time pressure and forced delay are weak levers. A claim 'intuition does X' built on time manipulations can be a selection artefact. Be careful trusting any S0 rule drawn from speed manipulations.

source: Gronchi, Gavazzi, Viggiano, Giovannelli (2024) Dual-process theory of thought and inhibitory control: an ALE meta-analysis
finding: Neuroimaging meta-analysis of dual-process tasks. Activation converged on medial and superior frontal cortex, anterior cingulate, insula and left inferior frontal gyrus, which overlap with cognitive-control areas.
numbers: Coordinate-based meta-analysis; study count not recorded here.
limits: Neural overlap does not show two separate systems. Authors call the common ground with cognitive control 'almost unexplored'.
agent_relevance: Low direct relevance. Suggests the split may reflect inhibition and control, which maps to checks overriding a default, not to two separate modules.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models (later: Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in LLMs but disappeared in ChatGPT)
finding: Older GPT-3 models fell for Cognitive Reflection Test traps like people. ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 mostly did not, mainly because they wrote out step-by-step reasoning.
numbers: CRT correct: GPT-3-davinci-003 5%, ChatGPT-3.5 59%, ChatGPT-4 96%, humans 38%. Intuitive (trap) answers: davinci-003 80%, ChatGPT-3.5 15%, ChatGPT-4 0%, humans 55%. Forcing davinci-003 to chain-of-thought: correct 5% to 28%, intuitive 80% to 29%. Blocking CoT in ChatGPT-4: correct 95% to 88%, intuitive 0% to 10%; ChatGPT-3.5 correct did not change significantly. Semantic illusions: davinci-003 fell for it 72%; ChatGPT-3.5 74% and ChatGPT-4 88% answered correctly.
limits: Trap-type puzzles, famous and probably in training data. Strong models solve many without CoT, so the effect is smaller than in older models.
agent_relevance: Shows the slow-mode gain from written reasoning shrinks as the model gets stronger. Supports a mode choice by model strength and task (G11, G12). CRT items are likely memorised, so use fresh variants.

source: Sprague, Yin, Brockett, Wu, Zheng, Durrett et al. (2024) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: Chain-of-thought (the closest LLM analogue of System 2 text) helps a lot on math and logic and little elsewhere. Almost all gain on MMLU comes from questions with an equals sign.
numbers: Meta-analysis of 110 papers, 1,218 comparisons, plus own tests on 20 datasets and 14 models. Mean CoT gain: symbolic 14.2, math 12.3, logical 6.9 points. Those three categories: 56.9 with CoT vs 45.5 without. Other categories: 56.8 vs 56.1. Up to 95% of MMLU gain from questions containing '='. CoT underperforms a symbolic solver.
limits: Mostly multiple-choice benchmarks and prompt-based CoT. Costs of extra tokens not matched in the comparison.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for S0: slow mode (written reasoning) is worth its cost on math, logic and symbolic tasks; for knowledge recall, a direct answer is as good. Medical diagnosis questions are mostly recall-like, so default to direct or short.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Griffiths et al. (2024/2025) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse
finding: Picked six tasks from psychology where deliberation hurts people, and tested CoT on models. In three tasks CoT clearly hurt; in others, mixed.
numbers: Up to 36.3% absolute accuracy drop for o1-preview vs GPT-4o on artificial grammar learning (implicit statistical learning). GPT-4o subset: 94.00% without CoT, 36.30 points lower with CoT (p<0.0001). Other tasks: face recognition and classifying data with exceptions (CoT hurt); natural language inference and others (mixed).
limits: Humans and models do not share mechanisms, so the human result is a heuristic guide only. Tasks are lab paradigms.
agent_relevance: Gives a method to predict when slow mode hurts: tasks where verbalising reduces accuracy (pattern recognition, exceptions). Fits G11. Useful for S0 mode rules.

source: Yu, Xu, Weston, Kulikov (2024) Distilling System 2 into System 1
finding: Outputs from slow multi-step prompting methods can be trained back into a direct model, keeping most of the gain with far fewer tokens. Fails on hard math.
numbers: Last-letter task: System 1 30.0%, 2-step Rephrase-and-Respond 44.5%, distilled 98.0% (unfiltered distil 87.5%). Coin flip: 56.1% base, 77.2% 2-step RaR, 75.69% distilled. TriviaQA with S2A: biased set 51.6% base, 76.0% S2A, 81.3% distilled (56 tokens versus 165). GSM8K: few-shot direct 7.58%, CoT 52.77% (k=1), zero-shot CoT distil 7.13%, so CoT could not be distilled.
limits: Needs training; our agent does not train. Self-consistency filtering was used to pick targets. Reasoning-heavy tasks (GSM8K) did not distil.
agent_relevance: Backs the claim that slow work should be spent where it cannot be compiled. For a no-training agent, a cache of verified answers or procedures is the nearest equivalent to compiling.

source: Weston and Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention (is something you might need too)
finding: Having the model first rewrite the input to remove opinion and irrelevant text, then answer from the rewrite, cut sycophancy and distractor errors.
numbers: LLaMA-2-70B-chat on opinion-laden QA: 62.8% baseline, oracle 82.0%, S2A 80.3%. Debias instruction alone 71.7%. Math with irrelevant sentences: 51.7% to 61.3%; random distractors gain about 12 points, in-topic about 10. Variant without separating context scored 74.5% vs 80.3%.
limits: One model family, 2023 setup; the context rewrite costs extra generation. It addresses distractors, not diagnosis.
agent_relevance: A concrete S1 input hygiene step with measured gain. A fixed rewrite step beat a 'be unbiased' instruction (80.3% vs 71.7%), echoing the human result that bias warnings are weak.

source: Schmidgall, Harris, Essien et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models (BiasMedQA)
finding: Added seven clinical cognitive biases to 1,273 USMLE questions. All six models lost accuracy; GPT-4 least. Bias warnings and examples helped a few points but did not restore accuracy.
numbers: Unbiased accuracy: GPT-4 72.7%, Mixtral-8x7b 51.8%, GPT-3.5 49.7%, PMC-Llama-13B 33.4%. Average drop under bias: GPT-4 -5.1%, Mixtral -7.7%, GPT-3.5 -17.8%, Llama-2-70B -20.1%, PMC-Llama -9.6%. Worst bias: false consensus -24.9% (GPT-4 -14.0%); frequency -18.2%; recency -12.9%; confirmation -8.1% (GPT-4 -0.2%). Mitigation: education +3.5 to +6.5 points on most models; GPT-4 few-shot mean 75.2%; GPT-4 recency one-shot 0.679 to 0.742. Education hurt cultural bias for some models (not significant).
limits: Multiple choice, prompt-injected biases, so it measures susceptibility to the prompt rather than natural bias. Weak instruction-following models barely gained. PaLM-2 refused 94 to 99% of one- and few-shot queries.
agent_relevance: Warnings help LLMs a little, unlike humans, but leave most of the loss. Stated hints in the prompt (patient self-diagnosis, others' view) are a hazard; strip or hide them (S1 input hygiene, G5 blind judging).

source: Wu, Xie, Gu, Kruger, Lin, Yang (2025) Why chain of thought fails in clinical text understanding
finding: On clinical text tasks, chain-of-thought lowered accuracy for most models. Drops grew with reasoning length and were smaller for stronger models.
numbers: 95 LLMs, 87 clinical tasks, 9 languages, 8 task types. 82 of 95 models (86.3%) worse with CoT. Best models still fell: Gemini-2.5-flash -1.6 points (-3.5%), DeepSeek-R1 -2.1 (-4.9%), GPT-4o -3.5 (-8.0%). 13 models improved by 0.1 to 2.2 points (10 under 1 point). Drop by capability quintile from -5.8% (top 20%) to -9.9% (bottom 20%), linear trend R2=0.973. GPT-4o relative drop widens by about 5 to 15 points from short to long reasoning.
limits: Text understanding and extraction on records, not diagnosis from cases. Prompted CoT; error analysis used LLM-as-judge plus expert checks.
agent_relevance: Strong clinical evidence for G11: default to direct answers on clinical text; do not add CoT on a schedule. Long traces are a warning, not assurance.

source: Moell, Aronsson, Akbar (2025) Medical reasoning in LLMs: an in-depth analysis of DeepSeek R1
finding: A reasoning model scored 93% on 100 MedQA cases; its 7 errors showed anchoring, poor handling of conflicting data, few alternative diagnoses and overthinking. Wrong answers had much longer reasoning.
numbers: n=100 MedQA cases, 93% correct. Mean reasoning length: wrong 8,118 characters vs right 3,648. Shorter answers (under about 5,000 characters) were linked to accuracy.
limits: Tiny sample (7 errors); qualitative error coding by authors, who may read bias in after the fact (hindsight, as in Zwaan). Single model.
agent_relevance: Long reasoning marks failure, which fits G10 and G11, so use length as a trigger for a check or a restart, not as a sign of effort. Labels such as 'anchoring' are after-the-fact tags that human work shows to be unreliable.

source: JMIR 2026 (e85770) dual-system pipeline: conversational model plus reasoning model under biased patient dialogue (seen only as a search summary)
finding: Per a search summary only: a conversational model as System 1 for history taking and a reasoning model (o1-mini) as System 2 for the final diagnosis improved accuracy under cognitively biased patient dialogue.
numbers: Search summary reports gains of about 10 to 39 percentage points across most models. Not verified; page text did not load.
limits: Not opened. Design, sample and baseline unknown. Treat as a lead to check, not as evidence.
agent_relevance: If confirmed, supports splitting intake from final decision. Do not rely on it until the paper is read.
